Empirical Research Plan – “Mariel Boatlift and Miami’s Labor Market”

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Chosen design: Difference-in-Differences (DID) complemented by an event-study specification.

Justification  
• The Mariel Boatlift is an exogenous, sudden, once-and-for-all shock to Miami’s labor supply in mid-1980.  
• We observe repeated cross-sections of individuals in Miami and in a set of comparable metropolitan areas (CMSAs) from 1979-1985, giving both pre- and post-treatment periods.  
• DID uses cities that did not receive large Cuban inflows as counterfactuals, differencing out common year shocks (e.g., Volcker recession) and city fixed characteristics.  
• An event study (year-by-year interactions) allows us to visualize dynamic treatment effects and to test the parallel-trends assumption.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable  
• Treated = 1 if an individual resides in the Miami CMSA (Miami-Ft. Lauderdale SMSA) during or after 1980q3; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
• “Synthetic control” set of comparison CMSAs that are large, coastal, Sunbelt, and pre-Boatlift demographically similar but received few Cuban immigrants (e.g., Atlanta, Houston, Tampa–St. Petersburg, San Diego, Los Angeles, comparable to Card 1990).  
• Alternatively, multiple-city DID with all other metropolitan areas except Miami; main results will emphasize the restricted, pre-matched set to maintain comparability.

Treatment timing  
• Event date: April–October 1980.  We code post = 1 starting with survey year 1981 (CPS is March supplement, reflects earnings over the previous year) and keep 1979-1980 as pure pre-period.  Event-study dummies will use individual calendar years 1979, 1980, …, 1985.

No running variable / cutoff because we are not using RDD.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel Trends  
   In the absence of the Boatlift, wage and employment trajectories for Miami’s low-skill natives would have moved like those in the control cities.  
   Plausibility: Reasonably strong—Miami’s pre-1979 trends in CPS can be checked; control cities selected to mirror Miami’s industrial mix and regional shocks.

A2. No Anticipation / Immediate and Permanent Treatment  
   Employers and native workers did not adjust behavior prior to April 1980 in expectation of the Boatlift.  
   Plausible: The exodus was largely unanticipated politically and logistically.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA) / No Spillovers  
   Labor-market shocks stay local; the Boatlift did not meaningfully affect labor markets in control cities.  
   Plausibility: Most Marielitos stayed in Miami; spillovers via migration of natives could violate this.

A4. Composition Stability  
   Within-city demographic composition (other than inflow of Cubans) is stable; survey sampling and coding are consistent.  
   Plausibility: We will restrict to prime-age native men / women and test for out-migration.

A5. Common Macroeconomic Shocks Fully Difference Out  
   Macro events (1981-82 recession) affect Miami and controls similarly after differencing year fixed effects.  
   Plausibility: Macroeconomic shocks may have heterogeneous effects across cities; include city-specific unemployment controls.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Endogenous Native Out-Migration (Selective)  
   • Threat: If low-skill natives leave Miami in response, observed resident natives overstate wage neutrality.  
   • Fix: Use CPS’s migration question (residence 1 year ago) to construct out-migration rates; run DID on person-level panel where available (Outgoing Rotation Groups). Instrument wages with city-year Cuban share in robustness.

T2. Differential Industry Shocks / Recession Heterogeneity  
   • Threat: Miami’s tourism & construction sectors hit differently by 1981-82 recession.  
   • Fix: Control for city-by-industry employment shares interacted with year; include city-specific time trends; restrict sample to industries least affected by recessions.

T3. Incorrect Control Group Choice  
   • Threat: Results driven by idiosyncratic controls.  
   • Fix: (i) Pre-Boatlift matching on wage levels and trends; (ii) leave-one-city-out tests; (iii) synthetic-control robustness.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # for high-dim FE regressions
library(modelsummary) # nice tables
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------------------
# Assume cps_79_85.csv contains one row per individual with variables:
# year, city, weight, wage, employed (1/0), hours, educ, age, sex,
# nativity, race, cuban, skill_cat (low, high)
cps <- fread("cps_79_85.csv")

# 2. Sample restrictions --------------------------------------------------
# Native workers aged 19-65, low-skill (≤ high school)
cps <- cps[nativity == "US" & age >= 19 & age <= 65 & skill_cat == "low"]

# 3. Define Treatment/Control --------------------------------------------
treated_cities <- c("Miami")              # Miami CMSA
control_cities <- c("Atlanta","Houston",
                    "Tampa","SanDiego","LosAngeles")
cps[, treat := fifelse(city %in% treated_cities, 1, 0)]
cps <- cps[city %in% c(treated_cities, control_cities)]

# 4. Timing ---------------------------------------------------------------
cps[, post  := fifelse(year >= 1981, 1, 0)]
cps[, event := year - 1980]               # event time for event study

# 5. Outcomes -------------------------------------------------------------
cps[, lnwage := log(wage)]

# 6. DID main specification ----------------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(lnwage ~ treat*post | city + year, 
                  weights = ~weight, data = cps, se = "cluster(city)")

etable(did_main, digits = 3)

# 7. Event-study ----------------------------------------------------------
# Interact treat with year dummies minus base(1979)
cps[, year_factor := factor(year)]
event_mod <- feols(lnwage ~ i(year_factor, treat, ref = "1979") | city + year, 
                   weights = ~weight, data = cps, se = "cluster(city)")
iplot(event_mod, ref.line = 0) + theme_minimal()

# 8. Robustness 1 – City-specific trends ----------------------------------
did_trend <- feols(lnwage ~ treat*post + city:year | city + year, 
                   weights = ~weight, data = cps, se = "cluster(city)")

# 9. Robustness 2 – Alternative controls set -----------------------------
alt_cities <- setdiff(unique(cps$city), "Miami") # all non-Miami CMSAs
cps_alt <- cps[city %in% alt_cities]
did_alt <- feols(lnwage ~ treat*post | city + year, 
                 weights = ~weight, data = cps_alt, se = "cluster(city)")

# 10. Save results --------------------------------------------------------
modelsummary(list(main = did_main, trend = did_trend, alt = did_alt),
             output = "results_table.html")
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Economic theory (simple competitive model) predicts that a sudden 7–8 % increase in low-skill labor supply (≈ the size of Marielitos relative to Miami’s workforce) lowers equilibrium wages of comparable natives and/or reduces their employment. Elastic labor demand and capital mobility mitigate effects. Prior literature (Card 1990) finds near-zero impacts.

Prior: A small negative effect. Magnitude: −2 % to −4 % on log hourly wages of low-skill native workers and negligible employment change, dissipating within 2–3 years as the market adjusts.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Parallel pre-trends verified graphically and statistically ........... 1  
C2: No anticipation of treatment ........................................ 1  
C3: No differential time-varying confounders ............................. 0.5  
C4: No spillovers between treatment and control areas .................... 0.5  
C5: Stable composition of treatment and control groups ................... 0.5  
Total = 3.5 / 5 – Reasonably strong but requires robustness work.

────────────────────────────────────────
End of Plan
